beats.n00: ஒமாஹாவின் ஒரு நீதிமன்றம். விசாரணையில், ஒரு நாளும் பள்ளிக்குப் போகாத ஒரு ஃபர்னிச்சர் வியாபாரி. குற்றம்? மிக மலிவாக விற்றது. விலை சட்டத்தை மீறுகிறார் என்றார்கள் போட்டியாளர்கள்.

beats.n55: மூன்று வருடம் கழித்து, தொண்ணூற்றொன்பது வயதில், Mrs. B கட்டடத்தை Nebraska Furniture Mart-க்கு விற்று மீண்டும் சேர்ந்தார். போட்டித் தடைக்கு அவரே முன்வந்தார். அவருக்கு எண்பத்தொன்பது வயதில் தான் கவனக்குறைவு என்று ஒப்புக்கொண்ட Buffett, உடனே பிடித்தார். பார்ட்னரே மேல்.
beats.n61: மோட்டுக்கு Mrs. B தேவையா? பிறகு நடந்ததைப் பாருங்கள். விற்பனை எண்பத்து மூன்றில் சுமார் நூறு மில்லியனிலிருந்து, தொண்ணூற்று மூன்றில் இருநூறு மில்லியன். இரண்டாயிரத்து பதினொன்றில், லாபம் Berkshire வாங்கியபோது இருந்ததை விட பத்து மடங்குக்கு மேல்.
beats.n62: சக்கரம் பயணித்தது. கான்சஸ் சிட்டியில் ஒரு கடை. பிறகு டல்லாஸ் அருகே ராட்சசக் கடை. இரண்டாயிரத்து இருபதில், அமெரிக்காவின் மூன்று பெரிய கடைகளும் NFM-உடையது, ஒவ்வொன்றும் சாதனை என்றார் Buffett.
beats.n62b: இரண்டாயிரத்து பதினொன்றில், ஒமாஹா கடையும் கான்சஸ் சிட்டி கடையும் தனித்தனியாக வருடத்துக்கு நானூறு மில்லியனுக்கு மேல் விற்றன. டல்லாஸுக்கு வடக்கே நானூற்று முப்பத்து மூன்று ஏக்கர் நிலம் வாங்கப்பட்டது, நாட்டின் மிக அதிக விற்பனைக் கடையாகும் என்று Buffett கணித்தார்.
beats.n63: Mrs. B? நூற்று மூன்று வயது வரை வேலை செய்தார். நூறாவது பிறந்தநாளில் கடை மாலையில் திறந்திருக்க வேண்டும். அதனால் பார்ட்டியை கடை மூடிய ஒரு இரவுக்கு மாற்றினார்.
beats.n71: இப்போது வாதம். ஒன்று. நிறுவனரின் ஆற்றலில் கட்டிய மோட் பலவீனம், Mrs. B கூட கார்ப்பெட்டில் தவறினார். இரண்டு. ஃபர்னிச்சர் உள்ளூர் வியாபாரம், ஒவ்வொரு புதிய நகரத்துக்கும் பெரிய கடை, நிலம் தேவை. மூன்று. குறைந்த செலவு மோட்டுக்கு நிலையான ஒழுக்கம் வேண்டும். ஒரு சோம்பேறி தலைமுறை, செலவு ஏறும். நான்கு. மக்கள் இப்போது புதிய வழிகளில் வாங்குகிறார்கள்.
beats.n72: எங்கள் தீர்ப்பு. Nebraska Furniture Mart மோட், தொழிலின் மிகக் குறைந்த செலவு, அதை மிகக் குறைந்த விலையாக்கியது, யாரும் தொட முடியாத அளவில். ஆபத்து, குடும்பத்தின் ஒழுக்கத்தை இழப்பது. நிலை? Berkshire வாங்கி கிட்டத்தட்ட நாற்பது வருடம், மூன்று சாதனைக் கடைகள்.
beats.n80: மலிவானது என்று சொல்லும் எந்த இந்திய சில்லறை வியாபாரத்துக்கும், மூன்று கேள்விகள்.
beats.n81: ஒன்று. விற்பனையில் நடத்தும் செலவு, போட்டியாளர்களை விட மிகக் குறைவா? இரண்டு. சேமிப்பை வாடிக்கையாளருக்குக் கொடுக்கிறதா, வைத்துக்கொள்கிறதா? மூன்று. நிறுவனர் இல்லாமல் இயந்திரம் ஓடுமா?
beats.n82: எந்த இந்திய கம்பெனியையும் சொல்லவில்லை. நீங்களே விசாரியுங்கள்.
beats.n83: நண்பனுக்கு ஒரு வரி. சேமிப்பைப் பகிரும் குறைந்த செலவு வியாபாரியே போரில் வெல்வார்.
beats.n84: ஒவ்வொரு தடயமும் Buffett கடிதங்களிலிருந்து. ஆதாரங்கள் டிஸ்க்ரிப்ஷனில்.
beats.n85: அடுத்த கேஸ். ஒரே ஒரு செய்தித்தாளை மட்டும் தாங்கக்கூடிய நகரம். இரண்டு பேப்பர்கள் போரிட்டன, ஒன்று வருடத்துக்கு மில்லியன்கள் இழந்தது. பிறகு போரை வென்ற மோட் கரையத் தொடங்கியது. கேஸ் ஃபைல் ஆறு. சப்ஸ்க்ரைப் பண்ணுங்கள்.

n00.say: It's a courtroom in Omaha. On trial, a furniture seller who never spent a single day in school. Her crime? Selling too cheap. Her rivals said she was breaking the law on prices.

n01.say: She proved she could sell carpet at a huge discount, and still make a profit. She won. And then, Warren Buffett wrote, she sold the judge fourteen hundred dollars' worth of carpet.

n02.say: Her name was Rose Blumkin. Omaha called her Mrs. B. She started with five hundred dollars. And every rival who fought her, lost.

n03.say: This is the case of Nebraska Furniture Mart. How did a woman with no money and no schooling build a moat that rich rivals couldn't cross? What exactly was the moat? And can a moat be just one person?

n11.say: Buffett told her story many times. At twenty three, she talked her way past a border guard to leave Russia for America. She knew no English. She learned it in the evenings, from her daughter, who taught her the words she'd learned at school that day.

n12.say: For years she sold used clothing. Then, in his early letters, Buffett says that in nineteen thirty seven she had saved five hundred dollars, and opened a furniture store. She named it Nebraska Furniture Mart.

n13.say: A detective note. In his twenty twenty letter, Buffett gives a different figure. Two thousand five hundred dollars, saved by nineteen thirty six. The amount changed. The point didn't. She started small, against rich and long entrenched rivals.

n21.say: Her rivals saw the danger quickly. She offered customers far better deals than they did. So they pressured furniture and carpet makers to refuse to sell to her.

n22.say: She found the goods anyway, by various strategies, and cut prices sharply. That's when they took her to court, under the old Fair Trade laws. She won every case. And the publicity was priceless.

n23.say: Once, when her money ran out, she did something no business school teaches. She sold the furniture and appliances from her own home, to pay her creditors exactly as she had promised.

n24.say: And look how thin it got. At the end of nineteen forty six, the company's net worth was seventy two thousand, two hundred and sixty four dollars. Cash in the till and the bank? Fifty dollars. Buffett added, no zeros omitted.

n25.say: Around then, her son Louie came home from the war. He had fought at Omaha Beach after D-Day, and earned a Purple Heart in the Battle of the Bulge. Once mother and son were together, Buffett wrote, there was no stopping them.

n31.say: By nineteen eighty three, that one store sold over a hundred million dollars a year, from a single two hundred thousand square foot building. No other home furnishings store in America came close. It sold more furniture, carpets and appliances than all its Omaha competitors combined.

n32.say: So what was the secret? Buffett compared it with Levitz, the biggest furniture chain in the country. Levitz's gross margin was forty four percent. Nebraska Furniture Mart's was not much more than half of that.

n32b.say: And remember, she had never been to school. In nineteen eighty four, New York University gave her an honorary doctorate in commercial science. Buffett joked she was a fast track student. Not one day in a classroom, before the doctorate.

n33.say: How could it charge so little and still earn excellent returns? Look at running costs. Levitz spent about thirty six cents of every sales dollar on wages, rent and advertising. Nebraska Furniture Mart spent about sixteen and a half.

n34.say: That's the moat. Lowest costs mean lowest prices. Lowest prices bring huge crowds. Huge crowds mean huge volumes. Huge volumes mean the shrewdest buying from suppliers. And that means even lower costs. Round and round.

n34b.say: Buffett later wrote the formula down, in five parts. The widest choice of goods, in one place. The lowest operating costs in the business. The shrewdest buying, helped by huge volumes. Prices far below competitors'. And friendly service, with family members always on hand.

n35.say: And here's the part rivals hated most. The family passed the savings on. Buffett estimated customers saved at least thirty million dollars a year, compared with buying the same goods at normal markups.

n36.say: Then Buffett asked his favourite question. If he had plenty of money and skilled people, how would he like to compete with this business? His answer. I'd rather wrestle grizzlies than compete with Mrs. B and her progeny.

n41.say: On August the thirtieth, nineteen eighty three, his own birthday, Buffett went to see Mrs. B. He carried a purchase offer he'd drafted himself. One and a quarter pages long. She accepted it without changing a word.

n42.say: No investment bankers. No lawyers. No audited accounts. No checking of property records. No warranties. Buffett's explanation? Her word was good enough for us.

n43.say: Berkshire bought eighty percent of the business. The family kept the rest, and kept running it. And Mrs. B, then eighty nine, didn't retire. She stayed on the sales floor seven days a week, selling carpet.

n43b.say: And the family? Her son Louie was, in Buffett's words, widely seen as the shrewdest buyer of furniture and appliances in the country. Louie said he had the best teacher. Mrs. B said she had the best student. Buffett said they were both right.

n44.say: Buffett even joked that he'd persuaded the board to scrap its rule of mandatory retirement at one hundred. Because at ninety four, she seemed to be just gathering speed.

n51.say: Now the twist. In nineteen eighty nine, at ninety six, Mrs. B fell out with her own family over how to run the carpet department. And she quit.

n52.say: Buffett wrote that Mrs. B had probably made more smart business decisions than any living American. But this time, he sided with the family. Over three years, the store's other departments had grown sales by twenty four percent. Carpet sales had fallen seventeen percent.

n53.say: So what did she do? She opened a brand new store, right next door, selling, what else? Carpet and furniture. Buffett had never asked her to sign a non compete agreement. The moat's builder was now attacking it.

n54.say: And the moat held. By the end of nineteen eighty nine, Nebraska Furniture Mart's carpet department had seventy five percent of the Omaha market. Six times its nearest competitor.

n55.say: Three years later, at ninety nine, Mrs. B sold her building to Nebraska Furniture Mart, and joined up again. This time, she offered to sign a non compete. Buffett admitted he'd been incautious when she was eighty nine, and snapped it up. Partner, he wrote, is better.

n61.say: So, did the moat need Mrs. B? Look what happened next. Sales went from about a hundred million in nineteen eighty three, to two hundred million in nineteen ninety three. By twenty eleven, earnings were more than ten times what they were when Berkshire bought in.

n62.say: The flywheel travelled. A store in Kansas City. Then a giant one near Dallas. By twenty twenty, Buffett wrote, NFM owned the three largest home furnishings stores in America, and each set a sales record that year.

n62b.say: By twenty eleven, the Omaha store and a newer one in Kansas City each sold more than four hundred million dollars a year. And Nebraska Furniture Mart bought a four hundred and thirty three acre site north of Dallas, for what Buffett predicted would be the highest volume home furnishings store in the country.

n63.say: And Mrs. B? She worked until she was one hundred and three. On her hundredth birthday, the store was due to be open in the evening. So she simply moved her party to a night when it was closed.

n71.say: Now the defence. One. A moat built on a founder's energy is fragile, and even Mrs. B got the carpet department wrong. Two. Furniture retail is local, so every new city means huge new stores and land. Three. Low cost moats need constant discipline. One lazy generation, and costs creep up. And four. People now shop in new ways, not just in giant stores.

n72.say: So, here's our verdict. The Nebraska Furniture Mart moat is the lowest cost in the business, turned into the lowest prices, at a scale no rival could match. Its threat is losing the family's discipline. And its status? Nearly forty years after Berkshire bought it, three record breaking stores.

n80.say: When you study any Indian retailer that claims to be the cheapest, open a case file with three questions.

n81.say: One. Are its running costs, as a share of sales, far below its rivals'? Two. Does it pass the savings to customers, or keep them? Three. Would the machine keep running without its founder?

n82.say: We're not saying any Indian company has this moat. You do the detective work.

n83.say: One line for your friend over chai. The lowest cost seller, who shares the savings, wins the war.

n84.say: Every clue here comes from Warren Buffett's letters. The sources are in the description.

n85.say: Next case. A city that could only keep one newspaper. Two papers went to war, and one of them lost millions a year. Then the moat that won the war began to dissolve. Case file six. Subscribe, and I'll see you at the crime scene.
